name: Molten-Altar
geological_features: Volcanic island arcs of solidified basalt
specific_features: A flat-topped basalt mesa at the center of the lava ocean used as a landing zone
Periodic planetary-scale eruption events that resurface entire hemispheres
description: Molten-Altar is a volcanic world whose surface is predominantly liquid, a planet-spanning lava ocean broken by islands of solidified basalt that form and dissolve on timescales of months to decades. The largest stable formation is a flat-topped mesa near the equator that has persisted for centuries, its dense basalt composition resisting the magma currents that consume lesser islands. This mesa serves as the only viable landing zone on a world where the ground is literally on fire, its surface scorched but solid, an altar of rock rising from a sea of molten stone.

The toxic atmosphere is dense with volcanic gases and suspended particulate, the heat so intense that unshielded electronics fail within minutes of surface exposure. The lava ocean glows orange and yellow across the spectrum, producing enough light that the night side of the planet is visible from space as a dim, ruddy sphere. Periodic planetary-scale eruption events, driven by mantle convection cycles that operate on decade-long timescales, can resurface entire hemispheres in fresh magma, erasing whatever geological record the previous surface held.

The geological violence of Molten-Altar serves a concentrating function for heavy elements, the repeated melting and recrystallization of surface materials progressively enriching the basalt islands in iridium, osmium, and other platinum-group metals. The mesa's longevity has made it the most enriched formation on the planet, its basalt containing ore grades that would be considered exceptional on any world. The challenge is not finding the metals but surviving long enough to extract them from a surface that is actively trying to melt everything placed upon it.

Mining operations on Molten-Altar are conducted during the quiescent periods between planetary eruption events, automated systems landing on the mesa to drill, extract, and launch ore into orbit before the next resurfacing cycle begins. The timing window is typically three to five years, and operations that misjudge the cycle length lose everything deployed on the surface. The iridium yields alone justify the risk, the metal's value in advanced catalyst applications and starship hull alloys making each successful extraction cycle worth billions. The altar continues its offering of metal and fire, indifferent to the small machines that come and go between its epochs of destruction.
